Learning Objectives
Identify the structural, cellular, and sarcomeric components of skeletal muscle.
Outline the processes that regulate volitional control of skeletal muscle contraction.
Identify the types of muscle contraction.
Assess various metabolic systems of energy production for muscle activity.
Identify skeletal muscle fiber types and determine how they respond to training.
Recognize the biologic processes involved in muscle development and growth, injury repair,
and disease.


Overview
Skeletal muscle is the largest organ by volume in the body and accounts for
approximately 30% to 40% of total body mass.1 It is primarily responsible for voluntary
mechanical activities, such as locomotion, posture, and breathing. In addition, skeletal
muscle facilitates various vital biologic processes, including metabolism, thermogenesis,
and the maintenance of homeostasis. The characteristic feature of skeletal muscle is its
plasticity—a robust capacity for adaptation throughout human life. Therefore,
maladaptive responses to external stimuli often result in muscle dysfunction and other
deleterious outcomes.
Muscle Structure and Morphology
Skeletal Muscle Fiber and Connective Tissue
A single skeletal muscle consists of groups or bundles of skeletal muscle fibers (fascicles)
(Resource 1).
A muscle bundle/fascicle includes hundreds of individual skeletal muscle fibers (myofibers).
Each myofiber has a single multinucleated cell and is a long, cylindrical structure, often
running the entire length of the muscle. An individual myofiber contains multiple nuclei
(myonuclei) and a bundle of myofibrils arranged longitudinally.
Individual myofibrils are held together by a collection of contractile filaments (myofilaments).
Adjacent myofibrils are connected to one another by specialized proteins called intermediate
filaments, which allow for mechanical coupling between the myofibrils.
Within a skeletal muscle, these collective structures are divided by three layers of connective
tissue into their respective compartments.
Epimysium is the outermost layer of dense connective tissue that surrounds the entire
skeletal muscle, thereby protecting the individual muscle and maintaining structural integrity
during contractions. Fascia resides outside this layer.
Perimysium is the intermediate layer of connective tissue that surrounds and separates the
fascicles. Other nonmuscle tissues, including blood vessels (arteries and veins) and nerves,
reside prominently within this layer.

Endomysium is the innermost layer of thin connective tissue that surrounds and separates
the individual myofibers. This layer is composed of basement membrane and extracellular
matrix. Besides allowing for myofiber contraction, this layer facilitates the metabolic
exchanges between muscle and blood.

Skeletal Muscle Fiber and Connective Tissue
Skeletal muscle is one of two types of striated muscle tissue in the human body, the
other being cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle is attached to a bone by a tendon and
consists of multiple integrated tissues (Figure 1). Skeletal muscles are enclosed by fascia,
a smooth sheath of connective tissue, which separates the muscles from other organs
and each other and enables muscles to slide smoothly past surrounding tissues.
Figure 1 Illustration shows the structure and layers of skeletal muscle tissue.
(Reproduced from Wright A, Gharaibeh B, Huard J: Form and function of skeletal muscle,

Skeletal Muscle Cell
The t-tubule system invaginates the plasma membrane and extends into the myofiber,
perpendicular to its long axis. Smaller longitudinal tubules extend from the t-tubules and
connect with the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Through this network, t-tubules are responsible for
the transmission of action potential, the electrical signal for muscle contraction, from the
motor neuron to the myofibrils.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum contains membrane-bound organelles and enzymes that
sequester, release, and reuptake calcium stores. Ion channels and calcium pumps facilitate the
influx of calcium into and out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In this manner, the sarcoplasmic
reticulum controls intracellular calcium levels in the skeletal muscle cell, which, in turn,
regulates the interactions between contractile filaments.

Skeletal Muscle Cell
An individual myofiber is a skeletal muscle cell with a plasma membrane (sarcolemma;
Figure 1; Resource 2). The sarcolemma extends into the cell and surrounds the
myofibrils. Myonuclei typically are situated at the periphery of the cell, in the space
between myofibrils and the sarcolemma. Residing between the basal lamina and
sarcolemma are satellite cells, the resident muscle stem cells.2 The unique structure of
the sarcolemma serves as an efficient system for activating muscle contraction, which is
regulated by two main components: the transverse tubular (t-tubule) system and the
sarcoplasmic reticulum (Figure 2).

Sarcomere
Thick filaments primarily consist of myosin.
Myosin is a large motor protein responsible for force generation in muscle contractions.
It consists of a long, insoluble helical tail domain, a site at which myosin molecules assemble
to form thick filaments.
Its globular head domain binds to thin filaments and hydrolyzes high-energy adenosine
triphosphate (ATP) into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) to release stored energy needed for
force generation.
Thin filaments include the cytoskeletal protein actin and the regulatory proteins tropomyosin
and troponin.

Thin filaments consist of two strands of the actin protein in a double-helix configuration, with
one strand of regulatory proteins situated between the double actin strands.
The two sets of filaments are arranged in parallel to another, in an alternating manner. The
overlap and interdigitation between the filaments allow for interactions between the actin and
myosin proteins, which result in muscle contractions.
The uniform arrangement of myofilaments within a sarcomere produces an alternating
pattern of light and dark bands, giving skeletal muscle its distinctive striated appearance
(Figure 3). Sarcomeres are organized as follows:
Z-lines are the borders of the sarcomeres and also serve as the attachment sites for actin
filaments.
The I-band is composed of thin filaments only, which connect to the Z-lines and project to the
center of the sarcomere.
The dark A-band runs the entire length of myosin and is composed of thick and thin
filaments.
The lighter H-band contains only thick filaments.
The M-line is a central set of interconnecting filaments for myosin and represents the center
of the sarcomere.

Sarcomere
Myofilaments are organized into defined structures called sarcomeres, which serve as
the fundamental contractile units of the skeletal muscle cell. Therefore, the largest
functional unit is the myofibril, which consists of a series of repeating sarcomeres.
Myofibrils are arranged in parallel along the axis of the cell, which ensures a cumulative
effect of contractions. Sarcomeres are composed of two major types of contractile
filaments: thick and thin filaments (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration shows a sarcomere, which is composed of thin and thick filaments.
(Reproduced with permission from Barrett KE, Boitano S, Ganong WF, Brooks HL:

Nerve–Muscle Interaction
All voluntary muscle activity, including muscle contraction, is regulated by the nervous system.
A motor unit consists of a single motor neuron and all the myofibers it contacts.
Each myofiber is contacted through a single nerve terminal at the motor end plate.
Therefore, if a motor unit is activated, all the myofibers within it contract (all or none law).
The number of myofibers within a motor unit varies widely.
The neuromuscular junction is the site at which the nervous system controls muscular
contraction.
It consists of the presynaptic axon, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle cell.
The neuromuscular junction serves as a chemical synapse for transmitting action potentials
from the motor neuron into the myofiber.
Muscle Function and Physiology
Muscle Contraction
The process by which muscle contraction occurs is elicited via interactions between the thick
and thin filaments, in a sliding-filament model.
In the sliding-filament model of muscle contraction, actin and myosin filaments slide past one
another, which leads to a reduction of sarcomere length and elicits subsequent contraction of
the myofibril (Figure 5). Therefore, muscle contraction results from the increased translation
of actin and myosin filaments relative to one another. The shortening of a sarcomere arises
from the increased overlap between thick and thin filaments because the actual lengths of
both sets of filaments remain unchanged. During muscle contraction, the structural
organization of sarcomeres is altered as follows:
The distance between Z-lines is shortened because of the reduction in the length of the
sarcomere.
The length of individual thick and thin filaments remains the same.
The A-band length is unchanged because the lengths of individual thick and thin filaments
remain the same.

The sliding filament model is molecularly driven by the formation and cycling of cross-bridges
between myosin and actin filament (Figure 6).
The myosin molecule has two heads or globular domains: one for binding to actin and the
other as a site for ATP binding.
On attachment to the myosin globular domain, ATP is hydrolyzed into ADP and inorganic
phosphate.
The energy liberated from this process activates myosin, changing the angle of its globular
domain into a cocked position.
The cocked myosin globular domain binds strongly to an available binding site on the actin
filament and forms a cross-bridge between actin and myosin.
Inorganic phosphate is subsequently released from the myosin globular domain, which
induces a conformational change.
The globular domain of myosin initiates a power stroke and pulls the actin filament toward
the center of the sarcomere, thereby shortening the sarcomere and eliciting a contraction.
ADP is released from the myosin globular domain at the end of the power stroke, leaving the
cross-bridge between myosin and actin intact.
ATP binds to the free site on the myosin globular domain to detach myosin from actin. This
allows myosin to bind to another actin molecule, thereby repeating the cross-bridge cycle
and eliciting additional muscle contraction.
The cross-bridge cycle repeats in the presence of a sufficient supply of cytosolic ATP.

Figure 6 Illustration shows the cross-bridge muscle contraction cycle. With each cycle, myosin
drives the sliding of actin filament. ADP = adenosine diphosphate, ATP = adenosine
triphosphate, Pi = inorganic phosphate. (Reproduced with permission from Cooper GM: Acting,
myosin, and cell movement, in The Cell: A Molecular Approach, ed 2. Sunderland, MA, Sinauer

A complex sequence of events involving intracellular calcium and the regulatory proteins
tropomyosin and troponin modulates the cross-bridge cycling process3 (Figure 7).
In resting muscle, tropomyosin blocks the myosin-binding sites on the actin molecules.
The position of tropomyosin is regulated by troponin, which consists of three domains:
troponin-C binds calcium, troponin-I inhibits the interaction between actin and myosin, and
troponin-T binds tropomyosin.
The binding of calcium ions with troponin-C induces a conformational change in troponin,
leading to the displacement of tropomyosin and the troponin complex from the actin
filament.
Myosin-binding sites on actin are subsequently exposed, commencing the active process of
cross-bridge cycling necessary for myofibril contraction.
If intracellular levels of calcium are exhausted, tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin
and halts muscle contraction.

The increase in intracellular levels of calcium is triggered by the depolarization of the skeletal

In response to signals from the nervous system, motor neurons release the neurotransmitter

Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the muscle membrane, which triggers a depolarization of
the sarcolemma and activates an action potential.
This action potential is propagated throughout the myofiber and into myofibrils by t-tubules.

Types of Muscle Contractions
Isotonic contraction
The amount of tension generated by the muscle remains constant while the length of the
muscle changes.
Can involve either concentric or eccentric actions.
Isokinetic contraction
The velocity of muscle contraction remains constant, whereas the length of the muscle
changes.
Can involve concentric or eccentric actions.
Concentric contraction
The amount of tension generated by the muscle is sufficient to overcome an opposing load.
This results in a decrease in muscle length during contraction.
For example, raising a weight during a bicep curl shortens the biceps brachii during
contraction.
Eccentric contraction
The external load placed on the muscle is greater than the amount of tension the muscle can
generate.
This forces the muscle to lengthen during contraction.
Eccentric contractions generate the highest tension and are associated with increased risk of
musculotendinous injuries and muscle soreness.
For example, lowering a weight during a bicep curl lengthens the biceps brachii during
contraction.
Isometric contraction
The opposing load is equivalent to the amount of tension generated.
Muscle is therefore held at a constant length during contraction.
For example, the length of the biceps brachii remains static when holding a weight at 90° of
elbow flexion.

Types of Muscle Contractions
The process of actin and myosin cross-bridge cycling generates tension (force exerted by
the muscle) in the myofiber. Depending on the amount of load (force exerted on the
muscle) it has to overcome, muscle responds by altering its length during contraction.

The length of the sarcomere at the time of contraction is therefore a key determinant of
the amount of tension produced during muscle contraction (Figure 9). This relationship
is governed by the degree of overlap between actin and myosin molecules. The greatest
overlap occurs if the muscle fiber is its normal resting length, which results in the
attainment of maximal tension. Conversely, shortening or lengthening a muscle fiber
reduces force production. Therefore, the different types of muscle contractions can be
defined by muscle length during force production.
Figure 9 Graph shows the relationship between tension and sarcomere length. The
greatest tension is attained at the normal muscle fiber length, when the overlap between
actin and myosin is greatest. (Reproduced from Huard J, Utsunomiya H, Ravuri SK,
Philippon MJ: Form and function of skeletal muscle, in Aaron RK: Orthopaedic Basic
Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 231-239.)
Graded Muscle Response
A muscle twitch is a single contraction produced by the muscle fibers of a motor unit in
response to an action potential from a motor neuron. Each twitch undergoes three distinct

AAOS | Biology and Function of Skeletal Muscle
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001004
18/45

phases.
Latent phase—the period after the activation of a motor neuron and before the start of
contraction. In this stage, the action potential propagated along the sarcolemma triggers the
release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to the cytoplasm.
Contraction phase—the period during which tension is generated and actual muscle
contraction occurs. In this stage, cross-bridges between actin and myosin are forming, which
results in the active shortening of sarcomeres.
Relaxation phase—this period is associated with a decrease in muscle tension because
calcium ions are sequestered back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, allowing the muscle fiber
to relax.
A single twitch does not contribute to substantial muscle activity, because work is performed
through sustained muscle contractions. If a second successive action potential arrives during
the contraction phase of previous twitch, the tension rises above the level of a single twitch
and leads to greater contraction of the motor unit. This phenomenon is called a summation.
During a summation of twitches, the second action potential triggers the release of more
calcium ions and forms additional cross-bridges.
Muscle tetanus is achieved if the frequency of stimulation increases to the extent that the
relaxation phase is bypassed between successive stimuli, thereby allowing for continuous
contractions to develop. This results in the sustained generation of peak maximal tension.

Graded Muscle Response
Muscle exhibits a varied response to stimulation from the nervous system in terms of
force production and tension development. The strength of a muscle contraction is
modified by the frequency of action potentials transmitted from a motor neuron (Figure
10). This association is known as the graded muscle response.

Muscle Bioenergetics and Metabolism
Metabolic Pathways
The phosphagen system is the quickest and most powerful source for muscle contraction
(Figure 11). It uses phosphocreatine/creatine phosphate stored in skeletal muscle as a rapidly
mobilized source of high-energy phosphate bonds.
The high-energy phosphate bond is dephosphorylated by mitochondrial creatine kinase. This
donates a phosphate to intracellular ADP, leading to the synthesis of ATP.
This system provides sufficient metabolic energy for 10 to 15 seconds of muscle contraction.
Therefore, it supports highly intense activities over a short duration that require the rapid
generation of power from the muscles, such as the 100-meter sprint.
This is a reversible process because creatine phosphate stores are replenished from unused
ATP.
Although this system is a form of anaerobic metabolism (does not require oxygen), it does
not produce lactate as a by-product.

Figure 11 Diagram shows the phosphocreatine system. ADP = adenosine diphosphate, ATP =
adenosine triphosphate. (Courtesy of Qingnian Goh, PhD, Cincinnati, OH.)
Anaerobic metabolism uses glucose, a form of carbohydrate, as fuel for energy (Figure 12).
Glucose usually is obtained and converted from muscle glycogen stores in the muscle fibers.
Glucose also can be provided by the bloodstream if glycogen stores are depleted or
unavailable.
Glycolysis, the breakdown of glycogen, occurs in the cytoplasm, and glucose is further broken
down into pyruvate, which yields two molecules of ATP per molecule of glucose.
This is the predominant energy system after 30 seconds of sustained muscle activity and can
provide metabolic energy for 20 to 120 seconds.
It supports short but intense activities, such as a 400-meter sprint or a shift in ice hockey,
which typically lasts 45 to 60 seconds.
In the absence of oxygen, pyruvate is converted into lactate at the end of this process.
Therefore, excess pyruvate can lead to the accumulation of lactate in the muscle. High levels
of lactate eventually lead to a systemic drop in pH, ultimately inhibiting the reactions that
drive muscle contraction.
Aerobic/oxidative metabolism (cellular respiration) also uses glucose as a potential energy
source for ATP (Figure 12). Of the three pathways, aerobic metabolism yields the most ATP
molecules but is less effective for rapid force generation.

After glycolysis, pyruvate is transported in the mitochondria of the muscle, where it is
decarboxylated and converted in acetyl-CoA. This is an irreversible process. Acetyl-CoA then
enters the Krebs cycle and is oxidized for a net gain of 34 molecules of ATP per glucose
molecule.
This is the primary energy system for sustained muscle activity lasting more than 120
seconds.
Therefore, it favors longer but moderate or less intense activities, such as most
cardiovascular exercises and activities of daily living.
Fats and amino acids also can be used as energy sources for ATP via aerobic metabolism.
The specificity of the energy system depends on the intensity and duration of muscle activity
(Figure 13).

Metabolic Pathways
Muscle contractions are primarily fueled by ATP, an energy-storing molecule. Hydrolysis
of ATP yields ADP and inorganic phosphate and releases stored energy necessary for
initiating cross-bridge cycling of actin and myosin. To perform additional contractions,
ATP stores must be replenished. Because intracellular stores of ATP are limited, ongoing
ATP production is provided by three main energy systems.4

Fiber Types
Skeletal muscle is a heterogeneous tissue composed of different types of muscle fibers.
This heterogeneity stems from distinct contractile, structural, and metabolic properties
of the myofibers and underpins the unique ability of skeletal muscle to respond and
adapt to various functional demands. The three general fiber types are grouped based
on contraction speed and predominant energy pathways: slow oxidative (type I), fast
oxidative-glycolytic (type IIA), and fast glycolytic (type IIB). A fourth group of muscle

The formation and maturation of muscular tissue is regulated by a highly ordered sequence of
cellular and molecular processes known as myogenesis6,7 (Figure 15).
Myogenesis commences with the activation of muscle stem cells, also known as satellite cells
because of their presence around the periphery of the myofiber.
These activated stem cells, also known as myoblasts or myogenic progenitors, proliferate,
differentiate, and fuse with one another to form nascent multinucleated myotubes, which
essentially are terminally differentiated muscle cells.
Myoblast fusion entails a highly regulated set of cellular events, including cell migration,
recognition, and adhesion.
Subsequent bouts of fusion between myoblasts and nascent myotubes, termed myonuclear
accretion, lead to myotube hypertrophy.
The formation of nascent myotubes and the ongoing addition of nuclei with existing
myotubes are primarily dependent on membrane union between the plasma membranes
of elongated myoblasts with other myoblasts, or myotubes.
Myotubes can further undergo hypertrophy via increased levels of protein synthesis.
The existing myotubes eventually mature into myofibers and align with other myofibers as
parallel bundles of fibers that span the entire length of the skeletal musculature.
Therefore, the muscle bundles/fascicles in mammalian skeletal muscle arise from the
assembly of multinucleated myotubes into well-aligned myofibers.

Training Response and Adaptation
Resistance training incorporates exercises characterized by high force production over a
relatively short duration, such as weight lifting. Therefore, it typically involves high-load and
low-repetition exercises.
Resistance training contributes to strength gains, which lead to increased force production.
This adaptation is associated with increased motor unit recruitment and/or improved
synchronization of muscle activation.
Resistance training also facilitates muscle hypertrophy in the form of increased muscle mass
and increased myofiber size. The latter adaptation occurs in all fiber types; however, type II
fibers display a greater capacity for hypertrophy.11 This leads to a greater amount of actin

become more efficient at using anaerobic metabolism as the energy source for ATP.
The hypertrophic response to resistance exercise is augmented by enhanced levels of
protein synthesis,12,13 which increase total protein content in the muscle. This improved
ability of muscle to synthesize proteins results from an increased activation of mammalian
target of rapamycin signaling after resistance exercise.14,15
The necessity of muscle stem cells for exercise-induced muscle hypertrophy has been a topic
of debate.16-18 Although findings from most recent studies seem to agree on a role for
satellite cells in hypertrophy,19-22 the mechanism for its contribution remains unresolved.
Specifically, whether satellite cells promote hypertrophy via fusion with the existing muscle
fiber (myonuclear accretion) or via direct cell signaling with the muscle fiber remains unclear.
Another topic of debate is whether the gains in strength can be uncoupled from the gains in
hypertrophy after resistance training and vice versa.
Other unresolved issues that may potentially provide valuable insights in training-induced
adaptations include the mechanisms that regulate myofiber length23 and whether
hyperplasia (increase in number of myofibers) occurs in postnatal human skeletal muscle.24
Endurance training involves exercises that generate a low to moderate force over a prolonged
duration, such as distance running. These exercises usually focus on increasing the oxidative
capacity of muscle fibers.
Endurance training results in changes in central and peripheral circulation and muscle
metabolism. Energy efficiency is the primary adaptation in contractile muscle because
endurance-trained muscles are more adept at using aerobic metabolism for ATP.25
Mitochondrial size, number, and density are all increased with endurance training.26 The
enzyme systems of the Krebs cycle and respiratory chain and those involved with the supply
and processing of fatty acids by mitochondria all increase markedly. This leads to the
increased use of fatty acids rather than glycogen as the main energy source.27,28
The increase in mitochondrial biogenesis is promoted by the protein, peroxisome
proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha.29,30 Specifically, nuclear
translocation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-
alphapromotes the initial upregulation of mitochondrial gene expression, whereas
subsequent upregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator
1-alpha expression leads to a sustained increase in mitochondrial biogenesis.31

Training Response and Adaptation
Postnatal/adult skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable capacity for meeting an
assortment of physiologic, metabolic, cellular, and molecular demands associated with
varying modes of exercise training. More importantly, it is capable of altering its
phenotype as an adaptive response to exercise training. This phenotypic plasticity and
other skeletal muscle adaptations are highly specific to the pattern of muscle activity
involved in the training regimen. In general, adaptations from strength/resistance
training lead to increased muscle size and improved neural activation. Conversely,
adaptations from aerobic/endurance training are usually associated with improved
metabolic function, such as increased mitochondrial density within the myofiber.
Muscle Injury and Repair
Muscle injury commonly occurs during physical activities and in almost all patients with
skeletal trauma. Muscle injury is usually is found in patients with a strain, contusion, or
laceration. Regardless of the mechanism of injury, the sequential order of biologic responses is
as follows: muscle degeneration and inflammation, followed by regeneration, and ultimately
fibrous scar formation (Figure 18).

Degeneration and inflammation
In a contusion or laceration injury, a compressive force or direct tear causes tissue
degeneration close to the injury site.
In a muscle strain injury, tensile force along the muscle typically causes rupture near the
musculotendinous junction.34
Mechanical injury usually disrupts the myofiber across its entire cross section, and necrosis
can develop along the entire length of the muscle cell.
However, condensations of cytoskeleton, called contraction bands, contain the injury at
regular intervals.35 The plasma membrane defect is sealed off within hours. Blood vessels
also are damaged, and hematoma develops.
Inflammatory cells infiltrate the site of injury directly through the damaged blood vessels
and are recruited via chemoattractants.36
Neutrophils are the predominant inflammatory cell during the acute period, and an influx
of monocytes follows 1 day postinjury.
These monocytes mature into macrophages that phagocytose the necrotic tissue before
tissue repair.

The neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, activated fibroblasts, and stimulated

Therefore, the main role of inflammatory cells is to remove damaged and necrotic muscle
fibers before muscle repair and regeneration.
The simultaneous formation of fibrotic connective tissue or scar tissue may interfere with a
full recovery of muscle tissue after injury.
Regeneration
Myofiber regeneration occurs approximately 1 to 4 weeks after the initial injury.
Adult skeletal muscle possesses a robust capacity for regeneration after injury because of
the presence of its muscle stem cell population, satellite cells.2,39,40
After the neonatal period of growth, satellite cells persist in low numbers but are normally
in a quiescent state. On injury, satellite cells are activated by growth factors released by
inflammatory cells, including fibroblast growth factors, insulin-like growth factor-1, and
hepatocyte growth factor.41
The activated satellite cells generate a pool of myogenic progenitors that differentiate and
fuse to each other or existing myofibers to restore structure and function to muscle9
(Figure 19).

Fibrosis
Fibrosis (collagen formation within the extracellular matrix of a tissue, such as a connective
tissue scar) begins with the cross-linking of fibrin and fibronectin within the hematoma to
create early granulation tissue.
Fibroblasts anchor to the granulation tissue and synthesize extracellular matrix
components.
Early strength and elasticity are provided to the granulation tissue by fibronectin, followed
by type III collagen. After several days, fibroblasts produce type I collagen, the major
component of mature scar tissue that gives it rigidity.
Fibrosis development and function are regulated by transforming growth factor-beta
signaling.42
Successful muscle repair after injury depends on the timely resolution of all three stages.
In acute injuries to heathy skeletal muscle, inflammation is rapid and controlled, and the
deposition of collagen is transient. This allows for efficient repair and replacement of the
injured myofibers43 (Figure 20).
In chronic muscle injury, the sustained presence of inflammatory cells, particularly the
different macrophage subtypes, alters the levels, durations, and interactions of various
cytokines and growth factors.36,44
These alterations perturb satellite cell function, leading to an impaired regenerative
response.45
Chronic inflammation also promotes excessive collagen accumulation, which leads to the
replacement of muscle with fibrotic/scar tissue.38,46,47 Therefore, aberrant fibrosis
development is a feature of many skeletal muscle pathologies, including dystrophy.43

Dystrophy
DMD is caused by mutations in dystrophin,49 a critical component of the dystrophin-
glycoprotein complex50 (Figure 21).
The protein complex provides structural integrity to the sarcolemma and stabilizes the
muscle cell membrane during contractions.51,52

Because dystrophin normally binds to cytoskeletal actin, its absence leads to the disassembly
of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex.
This compromises membrane integrity, which is further weakened during muscle activity.
DMD is marked by repeated cycles of chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling in the
muscle tissue, ultimately leading to myofiber degeneration.53
Because newly formed myofibers retain the genetic defect in dystrophin, they subsequently
undergo degeneration and perpetuate the degenerative cycle.54
Type IIX fibers are the first fiber group to degenerate.55 With progression of severity, all
voluntary muscles eventually experience weakness and wasting.
Models of DMD in mice have been used to study the pathophysiology of disease progression in
hopes of discovering a cure for this disorder.
This has led to the development of promising cell-based and gene therapies for the
management of DMD.56

Muscular dystrophies include a group of genetic diseases characterized by progressive
skeletal muscle loss and dysfunction. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most
common and aggressive form of dystrophy in children, with a low survival rate in
patients older than 25 years.48
Atrophy
Skeletal muscle atrophies during prolonged periods of decreased muscle activity and
stimulation, such as during denervation, systemic illness, limb immobilization, or bed rest.
The mechanisms driving muscle atrophy are a decrease in muscle protein synthesis and an
increase in muscle protein breakdown.57
Perturbations in mammalian target of rapamycin signaling may inhibit the capacity of
muscle for synthesizing proteins.
The increase in protein degradation may be attributed to increased forkhead box protein
O1 transcription of muscle ring-finger protein-1 and atrogin-1, two muscle-specific E3
ubiquitin ligases that target proteins for degradation.58
With aging, skeletal muscle gradually loses its regenerative capacity.59-62 In addition, aged
muscles undergo atrophy and experience diminished muscle function with decreased force
production, contraction velocity, and impaired relaxation.63 This aging-induced degenerative
loss of skeletal muscle is known as sarcopenia.
Sarcopenia (degenerative loss of skeletal muscle) is found in approximately 25% of
individuals aged 65 to 70 years and in 40% of individuals older than 80 years.64
Sarcopenia may be attributed to environmental or cell-intrinsic cues.
In aged muscles, the satellite cell pool diminishes and a population of satellite cells that
survive exhibit functional defects60,62 (Figure 22).
Resistance exercise training and nutritional supplementation may improve the results of
rehabilitation and reduce muscle wasting in disuse, aging, or disease states.65
